caveat: A mix of Timeline scroll, temporal zoom, historical jump and head reads, over a real socket on one developer machine — four cores, running PostgreSQL, Kafka and ClickHouse beside the service. What is worth reading is the shape across concurrency, not any single number: throughput rose nearly linearly from one reader to two and collapsed at four, where latency more than trebled. Above eight, ClickHouse reads exceeded the client's own ten-second budget and the service correctly refused — a finding about this laptop rather than about the code, and the reason the recorded range stops where it does. Comparable to another run on the same machine; not to anything else.

mix.name: open the head of a Timeline

saturation.observed: between 2 and 4 concurrent readers on this machine
saturation.beyond: at 8 and above, ClickHouse reads exceeded request_timeout and were refused
saturation.note: The projection was rebuilt immediately before this run, so parts were unmerged and every read paid FINAL over more of them than a settled projection would. ADR-147 records that read cost is a function of merge state; this is what that looks like under concurrency.
